title: Same-Origin Policy & CORS
objectives: Define an origin as scheme + host + port and explain what the same-origin policy blocks
Trace simple and preflighted CORS requests and their required response headers
Configure credentials, wildcard origins, and preflight caching safely
body:
# Same-Origin Policy & CORS

## The problem
Your bank tab and a random blog tab run in the same browser. Unrestricted, the blog's JavaScript could read responses from your bank session. The same-origin policy (SOP) prevents exactly that: scripts may only read responses from their own origin. But legitimate frontends must call APIs on other origins - CORS opens that door deliberately and auditably.

## What is an origin?
Scheme + host + port. Each pair below is a different origin:

```text
https://app.example.com  !=  https://api.example.com      (host)
https://app.example.com  !=  http://app.example.com       (scheme)
https://app.example.com  !=  https://app.example.com:8443 (port)
```

SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses. Embedding (img, script tags) is still allowed - which is why CSRF works against cookie-authenticated POSTs even with SOP in place.

## How CORS works
The browser, not the server, enforces SOP. CORS is the server opting in:

Simple requests (GET/POST with safe headers) carry an `Origin` header and get `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` back; the browser exposes the response to script only if the value matches.

Preflighted requests (custom headers, PUT/DELETE, JSON content types) add a step:

1. Browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` (and headers).
2. Server answers with allow-origin, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`.
3. Only then does the real request fly.

## Credentials
With cookies the request needs `credentials: "include"` client-side, plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and an exact origin on the server. The wildcard `*` is forbidden together with credentials.

## Failure modes that waste afternoons
- The server returns 200 but the browser reports a CORS error: the response was fine, the headers were missing. Read the network tab, not just the status.
- A redirect on a preflighted URL fails; fix the client-side URL instead of chasing redirects.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` plus credentials is rejected by spec.

## Decision framework
- First-party frontend and API on one domain? -> no CORS at all; prefer a same-site path or a reverse proxy.
- Public read-only API? -> `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is fine.
- Cookie-authenticated cross-subdomain setup? -> exact-origin allowlist plus credentials, with `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` to cache preflights.

## Best practices
- Keep an explicit origin allowlist in config; never reflect arbitrary origins blindly.
- Answer preflight `OPTIONS` with 204 and no auth requirement.
- Test CORS from a real browser; curl never enforces SOP and always looks fine.
- Remember CORS protects your users' browsers, not your server - keep server-side authorization.

## Common mistakes
- Debugging CORS with curl, which cannot reproduce the failure.
- Sending `Allow-Origin: *` while the client sends credentials.
- Allowing `Content-Type: application/json` requests but forgetting `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, so preflights fail.
- Treating a CORS error as a server 4xx; the request often succeeded server-side while the browser withheld the response.

examples.name: preflight.sh
examples.code:
# What the browser sends before a cross-origin DELETE
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/items/7 \
  -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: DELETE"

# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
# Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, DELETE
# Access-Control-Max-Age: 600

exercise.prompt: Implement check(allow, origin, creds): return "allowed" when the Access-Control-Allow-Origin value matches the request origin exactly, or when it is the wildcard and the request carries no credentials. Wildcard with credentials is "blocked: wildcard with credentials"; everything else is "blocked".
hints: Handle the wildcard case first: it is only allowed without credentials.
Otherwise a strict === string comparison against the exact origin decides.
Origins include the scheme and port; partial matches must never count.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the same origin as https://app.example.com?
questions.explanation: An origin is scheme + host + port; the path is irrelevant, so the /tools URL is same-origin while the others differ by host, scheme, and port.

questions.prompt: A cross-origin fetch that sends cookies requires…
options: An exact origin in Allow-Origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
questions.explanation: Credentialed CORS forbids the wildcard: the server must name the exact origin and explicitly allow credentials.

options: The browser blocks script access to disallowed responses
questions.explanation: The server only advertises its policy; the browser enforces it by withholding responses from script. curl ignores SOP entirely.
